title: India and China keep talking on their disputed Himalayan border, but troops stay put
summary: The 36th round in New Delhi on 6 August produced only a promise to keep talking, leaving disengagement complete but de-escalation undone and a new dispute over a giant upstream dam on the agenda.

claims.text: Early harvest proposal is a Chinese-origin concept to settle Sikkim sector first by replacing the 1890 Great Britain-China Convention with a new China-India agreement (first publicly floated by Ambassador Luo Zhaohui 2017, clarified by Sr Col Zhao Xiaozhou, formally submitted to Jaishankar Aug 2019). Indian historical position treated this as violating the 2005 Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles which envisages a package deal covering all sectors (Articles IV/VII on mutual and equal security and settled populations, implying as-is-where-is swap of Aksai Chin/Arunachal). The Aug 19 2025 SR decision to set up an Expert Group under WMCC to 'explore Early Harvest of boundary delimitation on appropriate Sectors' is therefore a departure from package-deal principle, with strategic risks cited regarding trijunction at Batang La/Jhampheri ridge, Siliguri corridor vulnerability, and Bhutan's Doklam interests.

claims.text: On buffer zones and disengagement, Indian official view (Jaishankar 3 Dec 2024 'disengagement achieved in full' clm_aca9aefaf4, patrolling restored to pre-May 2020 extents via coordinated patrolling) is contested domestically. Credible critics cited by International Crisis Group argue some buffer zones are 'carved more out of Indian territory than Chinese,' that New Delhi 'given away patrolling rights that it previously had,' that zones encompass grazing lands affecting Ladakhi livelihoods, and that zones are 'tantamount to territorial losses' requiring reciprocity and domestic justification. This dissent qualifies the profile's presentation of disengagement as unambiguously restoring status quo ante.

sources.title: Thin Ice in the Himalayas: Handling the India-China Border Dispute - International Crisis Group Report 334

claims.text: Claims that China's 'use of ambiguity as leverage' explains settlement distance and that 36th WMCC language is 'contradictory' and 'performative in not advancing' are interpretive attributions to Carnegie/ORF analysis (Threading the Needle, ORF Occasional Paper 508), not primary negotiating positions. Primary readouts announce no breakthrough (clm_bcef1113e7) but do not characterize talks as performative; Carnegie itself notes language is exploratory ('explore' early harvest) and that dual-track approach is new. Settlement distance also reflects mutual infrastructure build-up and 50-60k forward deployments on each side, not solely Chinese ambiguity.

claims.text: No new disengagement, de-escalation or delimitation agreement was announced at 36th WMCC; outcome was procedural commitment to continue dialogue (fact). Whether this reflects 'substantive channel-keeping' vs 'performative' stasis is inference. Distinguishing fact from inference, and attributing leverage/ambiguity thesis to secondary analysis while presenting Chinese delinking/early-harvest and Indian buffer-zone critique as competing credible framings, provides adversarial completeness.
